zh:
卷第四
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之四（內方便下分明驗惡根性）
en:
Fascicle Four
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
The Preliminary Expedient Means for Dhyāna-Pāramitā, Topic 6, Part 4 (the latter part of the internal expedient means: clarifying how to verify unwholesome capacity)

zh: 第二、明驗惡根性中，即有四意：一、先明煩惱數量；二、次明惡根性發；三、立對治法；四、結成悉檀，廣攝佛法。今釋第一、煩惱數量。煩惱者，《涅槃經》云：「煩惱即是惡法。」若具論惡法，名數眾多，今略約五種不善惡法開合，以辨數量。五種不善法者：一、覺觀不善法；二、貪欲不善法；三、瞋恚不善法；四、愚癡不善法；五、惡業不善法。
en: Second, clarifying how to verify unwholesome capacity: this itself has four parts — first, clarifying beforehand the number and categories of affliction; second, clarifying next the arising of unwholesome capacity; third, establishing the antidote methods; fourth, concluding by relating this to the siddhāntas, broadly encompassing the whole of the Buddhadharma.

Here, the first is now explained: the number and categories of affliction. As for affliction, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Affliction is itself unwholesome dharma." Were unwholesome dharma discussed in full, its names and categories would be manifold; here, in brief, the number and categories are distinguished with reference to five kinds of unwholesome dharma, opened out or brought together. The five unwholesome dharmas are: the unwholesome dharma of discursive thought; the unwholesome dharma of craving; the unwholesome dharma of anger; the unwholesome dharma of delusion; and the unwholesome dharma of unwholesome karma.

zh: 若開，乃有八萬四千，論其根本，不過但有三毒等分。若合，五不善法為四分煩惱者，三毒即守本，還為三分，並屬習因覺觀、惡業障道，此二不善，合為一分。所以者何？覺觀，即是帶三分煩惱而生，亦得說為習因等分。惡業障道，屬報因等分。習、報合論，但說一等分。故五種不善法，若一往合說，即但有四分，開論，即為八萬四千者，如《摩訶衍論》中所明：「貪欲煩惱具足二萬一千，瞋恚煩惱具足二萬一千，愚癡煩惱具足二萬一千，等分煩惱具足二萬一千，四分煩惱合出八萬四千塵勞。佛為對此說八萬四千法門為治。」
en: If opened out, these come to eighty-four thousand; discussing their root, however, they amount to no more than the three poisons together with the equal-portion affliction. If brought together, the five unwholesome dharmas form the four divisions of affliction: the three poisons remain as they are, forming three divisions, all belonging to the habituation-cause; discursive thought and unwholesome karma obstructing the path — these two unwholesome dharmas — combine to form a single division. Why is this? Discursive thought is itself brought forth carrying all three divisions of affliction within it, and so may also be spoken of as the habituation-cause's equal-portion affliction; unwholesome karma obstructing the path belongs to the retribution-cause's equal-portion affliction. Discussed together, habituation and retribution are simply spoken of as a single equal-portion.

Hence the five unwholesome dharmas, spoken of together in summary, come to just four divisions; discussed as opened out, they come to eighty-four thousand — as clarified in the Mahāyāna treatise: "The affliction of craving is complete in twenty-one thousand; the affliction of anger is complete in twenty-one thousand; the affliction of delusion is complete in twenty-one thousand; the equal-portion affliction is complete in twenty-one thousand; the four divisions of affliction together give rise to eighty-four thousand forms of worldly defilement. The Buddha, in response to this, taught the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates as their antidote."

zh: 今處中而明，是故但約五種不善惡法以辨惡根性發相。所以者何？上明善根性發，既約五種分別，今明惡根性發，豈不但據五不善法而辨？此則藥病相對，法相孱齊，行者欲修禪定，必須善分別之。
en: Here, a middle course is taken in the exposition, and so the arising of unwholesome capacity is distinguished only with reference to these five kinds of unwholesome dharma. Why is this? Since the arising of wholesome capacity above was already distinguished with reference to five kinds, how could the arising of unwholesome capacity now fail to be distinguished on the very same basis of five unwholesome dharmas? This is precisely medicine matched to illness, the two patterns held evenly together — and the practitioner who wishes to cultivate dhyāna-concentration must be able to distinguish this well.

The four-divisions-of-affliction scheme (craving, anger, delusion, and an "equal-portion" affliction, each at 21,000, totaling the traditional 84,000) already appeared in fascicle 3's note on the five-gate dhyāna; here the treatise supplies the reasoning behind it directly — the "equal-portion" division is itself a merger of discursive thought (a habituation-cause phenomenon) with unwholesome karma obstructing the path (a retribution-cause phenomenon), the same habituation/retribution pairing used throughout fascicle 3's account of wholesome roots, now doing the identical work for their unwholesome counterparts. The five-fold structure chosen here is explicitly a mirror of the wholesome-root scheme's own five gates — "medicine matched to illness" — so that every unwholesome mark that follows has a named antidote already waiting for it.

zh: 第二、次明惡根性發者，自有行人修禪定時，煩惱罪垢深重，雖復止心靜住，如上所說，內外善法都不發一事，唯覺煩惱起發，是故次明惡根性發。今就惡法發中，還約五種不善而辨，一不善法中，各自為三，三五則為十五不善法。若論行人發不善時，乃無的次第。今約教門依次而辨，具如前列。一、明覺觀發相，即為三種：一者、明利心中覺觀；二者、半明半昏心中覺觀；三者、一向昏迷心中覺觀。
en: Second, next clarifying the arising of unwholesome capacity: there are practitioners who, at the time of cultivating dhyāna-concentration, carry afflictions and karmic defilements so deep and heavy that, although the mind is brought to stillness exactly as described above, no single wholesome dharma — external or internal — is brought forth at all; only affliction itself is felt stirring and arising. Hence, next, the arising of unwholesome capacity is clarified. Here, within the arising of unwholesome dharma, the same five kinds of unwholesome dharma are again used as the basis for distinguishing it, each of the five itself opening into three, so that five times three gives fifteen unwholesome dharmas in all. As for the actual order in which a practitioner brings these forth, there is no fixed sequence to it; here, they are distinguished in the order given by the teaching itself, exactly as listed above.

First, clarifying that discursive thought has three differing marks of arising: discursive thought within a sharp, lucid mind; discursive thought within a mind half-lucid and half-dull; and discursive thought within a mind entirely sunk in dullness.

zh: 一、明利心中覺觀發者，若行人過去既不深種善根，於修定時都不發種種善法，但覺觀攀緣，念念不住，三毒之中亦無的緣，或時緣貪，或時緣瞋，或時緣癡，而所緣之事，分明了了，如是雖經年累月，而不發諸禪定，此為明利心中覺觀發相。二、半明半昏心中覺觀者，若人於攝念之時，雖覺覺觀煩惱念念不住，但隨所緣時，或明或昏。明則覺觀攀緣，思想不住；昏則無記瞪矒，無所覺了，名半明半昏覺觀發相。三、一向沈昏心中覺觀者，若行人於修定之時，雖心昏闇，似如睡眠，而於昏昏之中切切攀緣，覺觀不住，是名沈昏心中覺觀煩惱發相。
en: First, the arising of discursive thought within a sharp, lucid mind: if a practitioner has not, in the past, deeply planted any wholesome root, then, at the time of cultivating concentration, no wholesome dharma of any kind is brought forth at all — only discursive thought chasing after one object after another, never remaining still for a single moment. Even within the three poisons, there is no fixed object either: at times it takes craving as its object, at times anger, at times delusion — yet whatever object it takes is entirely clear and distinct. Even after years and months pass in this way, no dhyāna-concentration is ever brought forth. This is the mark of discursive thought arising within a sharp, lucid mind.

Second, discursive thought within a mind half-lucid and half-dull: if a person, at the time of gathering the mind in, still feels discursive affliction never remaining still moment to moment, but, depending on when an object is taken, is at times lucid and at times dull — when lucid, discursive thought chases after its object, thinking never settling; when dull, the mind is blank and glazed over, aware of nothing at all — this is called the mark of discursive thought arising within a mind half-lucid and half-dull.

Third, discursive thought within a mind entirely sunk in dullness: if the practitioner, at the time of cultivating concentration, has a mind dark and dull, resembling sleep, and yet, within this very dullness, chases urgently after objects, discursive thought never remaining still — this is called the mark of discursive affliction arising within a mind entirely sunk in dullness.

These three marks form a spectrum by clarity rather than by object — the same restless discursive thought (覺觀) that fascicle 3 named as what restraining-the-mind stopping is meant to restrain, here graded from sharp-but-scattered, through intermittently dull, to thoroughly sunk. Notably, even the "sharpest" version of this pattern is still classed as an unwholesome-root problem, not a wholesome one — clarity of mind alone, without any object of genuine wholesome content, is not itself progress.

zh: 二、明貪欲中即有三種發相：一、外貪欲；二、內外貪欲；三、遍一切處貪欲。一、外貪欲煩惱發者，若行人當修定時，貪欲心生，若是男子，即緣於女，若是女人，即緣於男子，取其色貌、姿容、威儀、言語，即結使心生，念念不住，即此是外貪婬結使發相。
en: Second, clarifying that craving has three differing marks of arising: external craving; craving both external and internal; and craving pervading every place.

First, the arising of the affliction of external craving: if, at the time the practitioner is cultivating concentration, a craving mind arises — if male, taking a woman as its object; if female, taking a man as its object — seizing upon their form, appearance, bearing, and speech, so that a fetter-mind arises, never remaining still moment to moment — this is precisely the mark of the fetter of external lustful craving arising.

zh: 二、內外貪欲煩惱發者，若行人於修定之時，欲心發動，或緣外男女身相、色貌、姿態、儀容，起於貪著，或復自緣己身形貌，摩頭拭頸，念念染著，起諸貪愛，是以障諸禪定，此即內外貪欲煩惱發相。三、遍一切處貪欲煩惱起者，此人愛著內外如前，而復於一切五塵境界資生物等皆起貪愛，或貪田園、屋宅、衣服、飲食，於一切處貪欲發相。
en: Second, the arising of the affliction of craving both external and internal: if, at the time the practitioner is cultivating concentration, desire stirs and arises, whether taking as its object the bodily form, appearance, bearing, and manner of a man or woman externally, giving rise to attachment, or taking as its object one's own bodily form instead, stroking one's own head or touching one's own neck, growing attached and stained moment to moment, giving rise to every kind of craving and desire, thereby obstructing dhyāna-concentration — this is precisely the mark of the affliction of craving both external and internal arising.

Third, the arising of the affliction of craving pervading every place: this is a person who is attached both externally and internally exactly as described above, but who further gives rise to craving toward every object among the five sense-objects and every article of daily necessity as well — craving fields and gardens, houses, clothing, food and drink. This is the mark of craving pervading every place arising.

The progression here — from a specific person as object, to one's own body added as a second object, to every object of daily life without exception — is the same expanding-scope pattern already seen twice in fascicle 3 (the five wheels, the three grades of the contemplation of impurity), now run in the unwholesome direction: craving does not stay contained to its original object but tends to generalize outward until it colors everything.

zh: 三、明瞋恚發相，即有三種：一、非理瞋；二、順理瞋；三、諍論瞋。一、違理瞋發者，若行人於修定時，瞋覺欻然而起，無問是理非理，他犯、不犯，無事而瞋，是為違理邪瞋發相。
en: Third, clarifying that anger has three differing marks of arising: anger contrary to reason; anger in accord with reason; and anger through disputation.

First, the arising of anger contrary to reason: if, at the time the practitioner is cultivating concentration, an angry thought suddenly arises regardless of whether there is any reason for it or not, whether another has actually done wrong or not, growing angry over nothing at all — this is the mark of deviant anger contrary to reason arising.

zh: 二、順理正瞋發者，若於修定之時，外人實來惱觸，以此為緣而生瞋覺，相續不息，亦如持戒之人見非法者而生瞋恚，故《摩訶衍》中說：「清淨佛土中，雖無邪三毒，而有正三毒。」今言順理正瞋者，即其人也。三、諍論瞋者，行人於修禪時，著己所解之法為是，謂他所行所說悉以為非。既外人所說不順己情，即惱覺心生。世自有人，雖財帛相侵，猶能安忍少諍，義理即大瞋恨，風馬不交，是名諍論瞋發相。
en: Second, the arising of correct anger in accord with reason: if, at the time of cultivating concentration, another person truly comes and causes disturbance, and, taking this as its condition, an angry thought arises and continues without ceasing — just as one who upholds the precepts feels anger upon seeing another act against the Dharma — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Within a pure buddha-land, although there is no deviant form of the three poisons, there is still a correct form of the three poisons." What is meant here by correct anger in accord with reason is precisely this kind of person.

Third, anger through disputation: if the practitioner, at the time of cultivating dhyāna, clings to the dharma of their own understanding as correct, taking whatever another practices or teaches to be entirely mistaken — then, since what the other person says fails to accord with one's own feelings, a mind of irritation arises. There are, in the world, people who, even when their own money or goods are encroached upon, are still able to remain calm and forbearing with little dispute, and yet, over a mere matter of doctrine, grow greatly enraged, refusing to have anything further to do with the other — this is called the mark of anger through disputation arising.

"Correct anger" is a striking admission — the treatise concedes that even a pure buddha-land retains some form of the three poisons, so long as it arises for the right reason, and that a precept-keeper's anger at witnessed wrongdoing is this same "correct" variety. Even so, the treatise still lists it here among the marks of unwholesome capacity that call for an antidote: arising and continuing without ceasing, correct anger obstructs concentration just as deviant anger does. Anger through disputation is aimed squarely at the treatise's own likely readership: practitioners calm about material loss but instantly enraged over a doctrinal disagreement, a pointed observation about where scholars' and meditators' actual attachments tend to hide.

quiz.q: Verifying unwholesome capacity has four parts. Which are they?
options: the number of afflictions, the arising of unwholesome roots, establishing antidotes, concluding with the siddhāntas
topics, marks, genuine or false, unfixed arising
three poisons, equal portion, three obstructions, four demons
quiz.why: "Clarifying how to verify unwholesome capacity: this itself has four parts — first, clarifying beforehand the number and categories of affliction; second, clarifying next the arising of unwholesome roots; third, establishing the antidote methods; fourth, concluding by relating this to the siddhāntas." The other lists belong to verifying wholesome capacity and to the internal expedient means.

quiz.q: Which five unwholesome dharmas does the text use to distinguish the number of afflictions?
options: discursive thought, craving, anger, delusion, unwholesome karma
quiz.why: "The five unwholesome dharmas are: the unwholesome dharma of discursive thought; the unwholesome dharma of craving; the unwholesome dharma of anger; the unwholesome dharma of delusion; and the unwholesome dharma of unwholesome karma." The five hindrances belong to fascicle 2.

quiz.q: When the five are combined into four divisions, how are discursive thought and unwholesome karma classified?
options: each its own division, five in all
discursive thought is craving, karma is anger
the two combine into one division, the equal portion: discursive thought as the habituation-cause, karma as the retribution-cause
quiz.why: "The three poisons remain as they are, forming three divisions, while discursive thought (belonging to the habituation-cause) and unwholesome karma obstructing the path (belonging to the retribution-cause) — these two unwholesome dharmas — combine to form a single division."

quiz.q: According to the Mahāyāna treatise, how are the eighty-four thousand defilements counted?
options: craving, anger, delusion, and the equal portion each complete in 21,000, together 84,000
quiz.why: "The affliction of craving is complete in twenty-one thousand; the affliction of anger is complete in twenty-one thousand; the affliction of delusion is complete in twenty-one thousand; the equal-portion affliction is complete in twenty-one thousand; the four divisions of affliction together give rise to eighty-four thousand forms of worldly defilement."

quiz.q: Why does the text take a middle course and use only five unwholesome dharmas?
options: since wholesome capacity was distinguished by five, the unwholesome is too — medicine matched to illness, the patterns held evenly
because there are only five afflictions
because 84,000 is too many to remember
quiz.why: "Since the arising of wholesome capacity above was already distinguished with reference to five kinds, how could the arising of unwholesome capacity now fail to be distinguished on the very same basis of five unwholesome dharmas? This is precisely medicine matched to illness, the two patterns held evenly together."

quiz.q: How many unwholesome dharmas arise in total in the arising of unwholesome roots?
options: each of the five opens into three, fifteen in all
quiz.why: "Each of the five itself opening into three, so that five times three gives fifteen unwholesome dharmas in all. As for the actual order in which a practitioner brings these forth, there is no fixed sequence to it."

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of discursive thought?
options: thoughts of desire, ill will, harm
in a sharp, lucid mind; in a half-lucid, half-dull mind; in a mind wholly sunk in dullness
quiz.why: "Discursive thought has three differing marks of arising: discursive thought within a sharp, lucid mind; discursive thought within a mind half-lucid and half-dull; and discursive thought within a mind entirely sunk in dullness."

quiz.q: What characterizes one in whom discursive thought arises within a sharp, lucid mind?
options: no deep past wholesome roots; no wholesome dharma arises, only discursive thought chasing objects, each object clear, and no dhyāna for years
quiz.why: "If a practitioner has not, in the past, deeply planted any wholesome root, then ... only discursive thought chasing after one object after another ... yet whatever object it takes is entirely clear and distinct. Even after years and months pass in this way, no dhyāna-concentration is ever brought forth."

quiz.q: In the half-lucid, half-dull mind, what is it like when dull?
options: blank and glazed over, aware of nothing at all
quiz.why: "When lucid, discursive thought chases after its object, thinking never settling; when dull, the mind is blank and glazed over, aware of nothing at all."

quiz.q: How does discursive thought in a mind wholly sunk in dullness differ from ordinary drowsiness?
options: there are no thoughts at all
though dark and dull like sleep, within the dullness it chases urgently after objects
quiz.why: "The practitioner ... has a mind dark and dull, resembling sleep, and yet, within this very dullness, chases urgently after objects, discursive thought never remaining still."

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of craving?
quiz.why: "Craving has three differing marks of arising: external craving; craving both external and internal; and craving pervading every place."

quiz.q: What does external-and-internal craving add to external craving?
options: also taking one's own body as object, stroking one's head and neck, attached moment by moment
quiz.why: "Whether taking as its object the bodily form ... of a man or woman externally ... or taking as its object one's own bodily form instead, stroking one's own head or touching one's own neck, growing attached and stained moment to moment." Craving for fields and houses is craving pervading every place.

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of anger?
options: contrary to reason, in accord with reason, through disputation
quiz.why: "Anger has three differing marks of arising: anger contrary to reason; anger in accord with reason; and anger through disputation."

quiz.q: What is correct anger in accord with reason, and what does the Mahāyāna treatise say?
options: anger at real disturbance or at seeing wrongdoing; "Within a pure buddha-land, though there is no deviant form of the three poisons, there is a correct form"
anger is good and should grow
quiz.why: "Another person truly comes and causes disturbance ... just as one who upholds the precepts feels anger upon seeing another act against the Dharma — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: 'Within a pure buddha-land, although there is no deviant form of the three poisons, there is still a correct form of the three poisons.'" It is still an unwholesome root to be treated.

options: clinging to one's own understanding, irritated when others disagree; patient over money yet enraged over doctrine
quiz.why: "If the practitioner ... clings to the dharma of their own understanding as correct ... There are, in the world, people who, even when their own money or goods are encroached upon, are still able to remain calm and forbearing with little dispute, and yet, over a mere matter of doctrine, grow greatly enraged."
